subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Paradox of Choice
description: Learn The Paradox of Choice in one minute.

hook.text: A grocery store offered 24 jams for tasting. Shoppers loved the variety—but almost nobody bought one.

buildup.text: When the display shrank to 6 jams, sales increased tenfold. Fewer options, more decisions.

discovery.text: Barry Schwartz called this the paradox of choice: more options create more anxiety and less satisfaction.

twist.text: With many choices, every option carries an opportunity cost. You imagine the roads not taken.

climax.text: Choice overload paralyzes the decision system. When everything is available, nothing feels right.

quiz.question: What happened when the jam display shrank from 24 to 6?

details.summary: Barry Schwartz argued that too many options can paralyze decision-making and reduce satisfaction. When faced with 24 jam varieties, fewer people buy than when offered 6. More choice increases regret, comparison anxiety, and the fear of missing out. Maximizers suffer most.
details.whyItMatters: The paradox of choice challenges the assumption that more options always improve welfare. It explains consumer paralysis and decision avoidance in an age of overwhelming choice.
takeaways: Too many options can reduce purchase rates and satisfaction
Choice overload increases regret and decision avoidance
Satisficers handle large choice sets better than maximizers

faq.question: What is the difference between maximizers and satisficers?
faq.answer: Maximizers try to find the very best option by exhaustively comparing all possibilities. Satisficers accept good enough and stop searching. Maximizers achieve slightly better objective outcomes but report less satisfaction because they compare and regret more. Satisficers are generally happier.

faq.question: Has the paradox of choice been challenged?
faq.answer: Yes. Later research found inconsistent replication of the jam study. Choice overload seems to depend on context: it is strongest when options are hard to compare, when preferences are unclear, and when stakes are moderate. When preferences are strong, more choice helps rather than harms.
